headline: The crossing is behind you and the first day off the trail is here. No run logged today — this is absorption, and that's the correct move. The story now is whether recovery signals come back cleanly.
confidence_reasons: Limited data sources active in last 3 days
confidence_attention: Limited data sources active in last 3 days

sections.overview: The four-day trail block dominates every load figure right now, and the picture immediately after it is one of deliberate emptiness. The last logged run was the short, very low-HR shakeout that closed the crossing; nothing new has landed since, which is exactly what a recovery window should look like. The recent four-week running volume is roughly double the prior block, but almost all of that jump is the crossing itself rather than a genuine step-change in weekly rhythm — worth remembering before reading it as a new baseline. Strength has been absent through the trail window, expected given the demands on foot, and its return is the cleaner marker of the block being absorbed than any single easy run. Steps remain high and essentially flat between rest and training days, so background load never really drops even when structured training does. The cardio-load status reads detraining, which here is an artefact of the rolling averages not yet catching up to the crossing — not a fitness statement. Sleep across the block was short and broken, unsurprising mid-crossing, and is the thing most worth watching for consolidation now.
sections.trends: Year-to-date distance is more than four times last year's mark at this point, which tells the real story: the base has expanded substantially and consistently across the season. The 16-week shape is cyclical rather than linearly building — normal rhythm punctuated by a large durability block — and that fits a hybrid athlete maintaining year-round readiness rather than periodising toward one date. The recent doubling of volume is a single event spike, not a trend inflection; expect the weekly figure to settle back once the crossing rolls out of the window. Nothing here suggests either overreaching or drift.
sections.threshold: Threshold pace and its anchoring HR are unchanged from the early-July test, so there's no new aerobic data to interpret — and none should be expected from a block spent entirely at controlled, low-HR durability pace. The trail work builds a different quality than threshold sharpness, and a flat threshold marker through it is neither a gain nor a loss. The relevant question is what threshold work looks like once speed sessions re-enter, not what the number does during recovery.
sections.zones: The per-session shapes across the crossing are almost entirely Z1, with only small Z2 touches on the two biggest days — precisely the controlled-intensity distribution an ultra durability block should produce. There's no grey-zone creep and essentially no Z3+ anywhere in the block, confirming the effort was managed on HR rather than pace throughout. That discipline is the point: hours on feet without accumulating intensity cost. As normal rhythm returns, the distribution will need to reopen toward some genuine Z4/Z5 work to keep speed capacity alive, but during absorption the near-total Z1 profile is correct.
sections.hr_comparison: Nothing genuinely notable in the strength HR patterns right now, since no strength has been logged inside the trail window — the most recent sessions sit in their usual low-to-moderate band. On the two H10-dropout runs from early August, the estimated and expected effort levels line up sensibly with pace, so there's no source-disagreement worth flagging.
sections.calendar: The recent calendar is unusually clustered — four consecutive foot days, then a gap — which is the opposite of the athlete's normal spread-out four-runs-plus-strength week. That clustering is the crossing, not a change in habit, and the gap after it is intentional. What's worth watching is how quickly the calendar returns to its usual interleaved shape; a prompt return signals clean absorption, while a prolonged gap would suggest the block cost more than the low HR implied.
sections.personal_bests: No bests are in play during a recovery window, and the current durability focus sits at the opposite end of the spectrum from the short-distance PBs. Those speed marks will only become relevant again once fast sessions return and threshold work resumes — nothing to chase here now.

watch_items: Watch whether the first easy runs back show elevated HR at normal pace, which would indicate the crossing is still being paid down.
Watch when strength re-enters the log — its return is the clearest marker that the block has been absorbed and normal rhythm has resumed.
Watch whether sleep consolidates now that the crossing window has closed, since the block's nights were short and broken.
Watch whether the calendar returns to its usual interleaved spread rather than staying sparse, as a prolonged gap would hint at a higher recovery cost than the low HR suggested.
